# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up. It answers the open questions from the nine-month report with better measures:
- log-based hours,
- a registered mediation test,
- 24-month follow-up,
- an honest account of the terminated counter arm.

Its rebuttals of the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are mostly well founded. I checked the arithmetic and it is consistent:
- **Varden, timesheet hours:** 0.966 ÷ 0.88 gives +9.8%.
- **Varden, log hours:** 0.966 ÷ 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- **Halden subset:** 34.9 ÷ 40.3 gives −13.4%, and 0.968 ÷ 0.866 gives +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares:** 47 + 18 + 35 sum to 100.

The issues below are mostly about calibration, plus one possible design gap.

## 1. The Summary compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months."
- 12.5% is the timesheet-based estimate. 8.5% is log-based.
- The like-for-like comparison, which the body correctly uses, is 12.5% → 9.8%.

As written, the Summary overstates the decline by mixing in the change of measure. The fix is to report both figures with their measures named.

## 2. The decline is not statistically established, and the control group was partly contaminated

**Overlapping intervals.**
- The nine-month CI runs from +6.9% to +18.4%, and the 24-month timesheet CI from +4.6% to +15.2%. They overlap heavily.
- "Consistent with some fading" is fair.
- Section 5's flat statement that the gain "declined by about a quarter" is stronger than the data allow. (Also, 12.5 → 9.8 is a fall of about 22%.)

**Control-office contamination.**
- Two of the seven control offices ran a meeting audit in month 15 and saw output per hour about 4.1% above their own previous six months.
- If that change is real, it raises the control average by roughly 1 point, which narrows the treated–control gap.
- So part of the apparent decline may be the control group improving, not the treatment effect fading.
- This should be discussed. A sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices from month 15 onward would show how much it matters.

**Likely source of the contamination.** The audit plausibly followed publicity of the nine-month meetings finding. That is a spillover from the trial's own results, and worth naming.

## 3. The mediation result is less independent than "confirms" implies

**Same offices.** The hypothesis came from the seven treated case-processing offices at month six, and the registered test uses those same seven offices over a period that includes the months that produced the hypothesis.
- It is a pre-specified test, which is an improvement, but it is not an independent replication.
- Re-running it on months 10–24 only would be the cleanest available check.

**Cluster count.** "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't add independent units. With 7 against 7 offices, mediation shares with intervals as tight as 28–66% need explaining.
- How was clustering handled?
- Was the few-cluster problem addressed, for example through randomisation inference or a bootstrap at office level?

**Confounding.** The Limitations section notes it, but it deserves a concrete example.
- Meeting cuts were chosen by managers. More effective managers may both cut meetings and raise output, which is exactly the mediator–outcome confounding the method can't rule out.
- That makes "confirms" too strong for the Summary. The body's "survives a registered test" is the right wording.

**Unexplained share.** The 35% unexplained share needs an interval.

## 4. What do log hours measure, and from when?

**Scope.**
- Log-in time on the case-management system captures case work, but probably not meetings, phone calls or paper work.
- If so, output per log hour is output per hour of *case work*. Cutting meetings wouldn't reduce that denominator directly.
- The mediation result would then have to work through focus or fewer interruptions rather than freed-up time. That is an interesting finding, but a different one from the obvious reading.
- Please state exactly what log time includes.

**Baseline.**
- The log measure was "added" at follow-up, and Table 1 shows "—" at nine months.
- A difference-in-differences estimate of −11% requires pre-period log data.
- If historical logs were retrieved, say so. If not, the log-based figures aren't difference-in-differences estimates.

## 5. The Halden subset

**Reverting organisations.**
- The Summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations." But one is a marketing agency citing client deadlines.
- That is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's coding. Grouping it with coverage-bound settings makes the work-type split look tidier than it is, and it should be reported as a discretionary-sector reversion.

**Non-response.**
- 9 of the 23 organisations didn't respond, and organisations that struggled or reverted may be less willing to provide data.
- The sentence "an upper bound for organisations that self-select" is good. However, without a comparison group, two years of general productivity change (new tools, a changing workload) is also included, so "upper bound" is a judgement, not a guarantee.

**Minor.** The 11 continuing organisations have a baseline of exactly 40.3 hours, the same as the re-analysis's 27-organisation figure. Worth confirming that this isn't a carry-over.

## 6. Earlier claims are addressed unevenly

Section 5 addresses the re-analysis and the meta-analysis directly and fairly. It does not address the original Halden working paper's claims:
- the 23.4% headline,
- "sector-general,"
- the discrepancy over attrition, where the microdata show withdrawals *after* the schedule began, not during preparation.

With a Halden author now on the team, this report is a natural place to correct or explain those points. Leaving them out while rebutting both critics makes the section look one-sided, even though the substance of the rebuttals is right.

## 7. Points still open from the nine-month report

- **Sick days.** Is the −27% per scheduled day or per year? The mechanical-reduction question remains.
- **Resignations and appeal overturn rates.** These still have no intervals. Overturn rates are now less right-censored, which is good, but should still come with CIs.
- **Few-cluster inference.** Randomisation inference or a wild cluster bootstrap is not mentioned for the main estimates.
- **Costs for case-processing.** A cost per contact (+9%) is now given for the counter arm, but not for case-processing, where overtime continues on top of full pay. Readers asking "does it pay?" will want both.
- **Backlog and case mix.** The Limitations section of the nine-month report raised the risk that backlogs build up beyond statutory deadlines. Queue length and time-to-decision should be reported at 24 months.

## 8. Smaller points

- **The unplanned observation is well caveated.** One addition: compare the two auditing offices with the other five control offices over the same months, rather than only with their own previous six months. That would deal with seasonality.
- **Rebuttal of the re-analysis.** "Not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten" is fair. Note that the re-analysis extrapolated from Halden survey data, not Varden data, so this is a test of the general claim rather than of that specific extrapolation.
- **Counter arm termination.** The judgement that restoring service would need about 12% more staff fits the nine-month per-FTE loss (1 ÷ 0.886 is about 1.13). It's a helpful consistency check worth stating.

## A suggested Summary

> At 24 months, the per-hour gain in Varden case-processing offices relative to control was 9.8% on timesheet hours (12.5% at nine months) and 8.5% on system-log hours, with output per employee at −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2). The decline from nine months is within sampling error and may partly reflect a meeting audit in two control offices. A mediation analysis, pre-registered at month 11 and conducted in the same offices that generated the hypothesis, attributes about half the gain to reduced meetings and about a fifth to reduced fatigue, subject to the usual assumption of no unmeasured confounding. The counter arm was ended at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of 14 Halden organisations providing follow-up data had reverted, including one discretionary-sector firm.

## Bottom line

The core findings look solid:
- a durable but modest per-hour gain, of high single digits;
- slightly lower output per employee in backlog work;
- clear failure in coverage-bound work.

The changes most needed are:
- fixing the Summary's comparison of mismatched measures;
- softening "confirms" and "declined by about a quarter";
- clarifying what log hours measure and whether a pre-period exists;
- dealing with the control-office contamination;
- giving the original Halden claims the same direct treatment as the two critiques.
